Empirical Research Plan ― Estimating a Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) under Self-Selection

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen design: Instrumental-Variables (IV), implemented as two–stage least squares (2SLS).

Justification  
• Individuals self-select into treatment, so simple comparisons are biased.  
• A valid instrument Z that shifts the probability of treatment (T) but affects the outcome (Y) only through T isolates exogenous treatment variation.  
• Under the standard IV assumptions, 2SLS identifies the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for compliers—exactly the causal parameter of interest in self-selection settings with heterogeneous effects.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
Tᵢ = 1 if individual i received the program/policy (treated), 0 otherwise.

Instrument  
Zᵢ = 1 if individual i was exposed to the exogenous inducement (e.g., eligibility date, lottery win, distance cutoff, policy rollout cohort), 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Individuals with T = 0 serve as the baseline. Within that group, some have Z = 0 (never-takers) and some have Z = 1 (would-be compliers but did not take-up).

Timing  
If the inducement is a policy change, treatment timing equals the date the policy became available to a given unit. For cross-sectional instruments (e.g., lottery), timing is implicit in the instrument.

(There is no running variable/cutoff typical of RDD.)

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions (IV)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Relevance: Cov(Z, T) ≠ 0.  
 Plausibility: Policy or lottery instruments usually generate a strong first stage.

A2. Independence (Unconfoundedness of Z): Z ⊥ (U, ε), where U and ε are unobservables determining T and Y.  
 Plausibility: Credible if Z is assigned by rule or chance (e.g., lottery, staggered rollout not targeted on potential outcomes).

A3. Exclusion Restriction: Z affects Y only through T.  
 Plausibility: Must argue that the policy inducement has no direct effect on the outcome (e.g., eligibility notice itself does not change Y).

A4. Monotonicity: No defiers; Z can only weakly increase the probability of treatment for every unit.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable for eligibility rules or distance instruments.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): No interference and single version of treatment.  
 Plausibility: Requires that one person’s inducement doesn’t affect another’s outcome and that treatment is well-defined.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Threat 1. Weak Instrument (violates A1)  
• Check F-statistic (> 10 rule of thumb) in first stage.  
• If weak, search for stronger variant or combine multiple instruments.

Threat 2. Violation of Exclusion (A3)  
• Provide institutional argument; test for direct effects on pre-treatment outcomes (placebo outcomes or leads).  
• Include controls for any channels through which Z could directly affect Y.

Threat 3. Heterogeneous treatment timing causing differential trends (if panel)  
• Add time and unit fixed effects; interact time dummies with Z if necessary.  
• Restrict to narrow windows around the policy change to equalize trends.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 1. Load libraries
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # IV regressions & clustered SEs
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov
library(lmtest)       # hypothesis tests
# install.packages(c("data.table","fixest","sandwich","lmtest")) if needed

# 2. Load data
df <- fread("analysis_data.csv")   # assumes variables: id, Y, T, Z, X1, X2, ...

# 3. Variable construction
df[, `:=`(
  treat = as.integer(T),           # ensure 0/1 numeric
  inst  = as.integer(Z)
)]

# 4. Main specification: 2SLS with controls and clustered SEs
iv_main <- feols(Y ~ X1 + X2 | inst ~ treat, cluster = ~cluster_id, data = df)
summary(iv_main, cluster = "cluster_id")

# 5. First-stage diagnostics (weak-instrument test)
summary(iv_main, stage = 1)$fs # F-statistic and partial R²

# 6. Robustness check 1: add additional controls
iv_robust1 <- feols(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 | inst ~ treat, cluster = ~cluster_id, data = df)

# 7. Robustness check 2: placebo outcome (Y_placebo)
iv_placebo <- feols(Y_placebo ~ X1 + X2 | inst ~ treat, cluster = ~cluster_id, data = df)

# 8. Over-identification test (if multiple instruments)
# Suppose we added inst2 and inst3 to | inst + inst2 + inst3
# wald_iv <- wald(iv_multi)   # Sargan/Hansen test via fixest
```

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory suggests the treatment is beneficial (e.g., training increases earnings), so I expect a positive effect on Y. Magnitude: roughly 5–10 % increase in the outcome variable for compliers, but exact size is context-specific.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1 (Relevance)………………1  
C2 (Independence)…………0.5 (needs strong institutional case)  
C3 (Exclusion Restriction)..0.5 (must be argued and placebo-tested)  
C4 (Monotonicity)……………1  
C5 (SUTVA)…………………0.5 (plausible but untestable)

Overall: 3.5 / 5 ─ reasonable but hinges on defending exclusion and no interference.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
